issues.issue: The preamble assigns CSi Agency Services the defined short name "CS" while the rest of the instrument uses "CSi", and the parenthetical for Alpha Partners is malformed ("Alpha Partners, Ltd, Alpha")). These are mechanical slips in the definitional apparatus, though the intended referents are obvious from context.

The recital defines "the reinsurance relationship" by an enumerated list of agreements and addenda prefaced by "including, but not limited to," leaving the reach of the catch-all over other addenda uncertain. It also names State and County Mutual as a party to that relationship though it is not a party to this MOU.

The recital's defined "reinsurance relationship" is never used in the operative sections, which instead recite the individual agreements (Sections I and III), so the two descriptions of scope must be harmonised. No square contradiction appears.

The recital says the business solution "involves the payment, going forward, beginning May 4, 2009, of losses and all fees and expenses and costs associated in any way with" the reinsured policies without saying who must pay, and "associated in any way" has no discernible boundary. The payor and the outer edge of the covered costs are both left to construction.

The recital's picture of a global forward-looking payment solution sits against Section III's final sentence, which preserves "any obligations of U.S. Auto, Gamma, or any other defendant," so the recital may be read to allocate to Santa Fe what the operative text leaves open. A court could be asked whether the recital colours Sections I and III.

The obligation is to "enter into" an LPT whose terms are not set out here, so whether this is a binding transfer of liability or only an agreement to agree turns on words outside the clause. "All past and future losses ... whether or not known" is broad but is not itself indefinite.

Section IX describes the same instrument as a "mutually agreeable reinsurance agreement/LPT" whose non-completion merely lets Lincoln refile, which pulls against the mandatory "shall enter into" here and against Section V's stipulation that the MOU is enforceable. Reconciling the command with the escape hatch is a genuine construction problem.

The carve-out for "payments completed prior to May 4, 2009" does not say whose payments, and the following sentence defines completion only by reference to checks issued by Santa Fe. The exclusion's application to payments made by Lincoln General is therefore uncertain.

The exclusion must be squared with the ZBA reimbursement sentence of Section I, which makes Santa Fe reimburse "all payments out of the ZBA from May 4, 2009," leaving the treatment of checks issued before but cleared after that date contestable. The two sentences use different payment concepts.

The definition says "a payment is considered to have been 'completed' when the check or payment has been dated and issued by Santa Fe," so a payment made by anyone other than Santa Fe has no defined completion date. Whether "dated and issued" requires both, and on which date, is also open.

Because Section I elsewhere speaks of payments out of Lincoln General's ZBA, the Santa Fe-only definition cannot be applied to those payments without strain. The definition and the ZBA reimbursement sentence assume different payors.
The permission runs "until the LPT is executed, but no later than June 30, 2009," which does not say what happens to claim payments if the LPT is not executed by that date. The gap is real but small.

Section IX contemplates that the LPT may never be executed, yet this clause cuts off ZBA use on June 30, 2009 regardless, leaving claims funding unaddressed in that interval. The two provisions assume different futures.

"The date of execution" is unqualified and could refer to execution of the LPT (the subject of the preceding sentence) or of the MOU itself. The date on which the ZBA must go dark turns on which is meant.

The reimbursement window runs "from May 4, 2009 until the date of execution," repeating the unqualified phrase "the date of execution" (LPT or MOU), so the end of Santa Fe's reimbursement obligation is uncertain. No timing or mechanism for reimbursement is stated either.

The obligation to reimburse "all payments out of the ZBA from May 4, 2009" overlaps with the Section I carve-out for payments "completed" before May 4, 2009, and the two use inconsistent tests for when a payment counts. A court could be asked to reconcile them.

"Other investments acceptable to Lincoln General" and "an A rated reinsurer" are both undefined — the first gives unbounded discretion with no reasonableness qualifier, the second does not identify the rating agency or the timing of the rating. Either could be read differently by the parties.

Elsewhere in Section II Lincoln General's approvals are expressly qualified as "not to be unreasonably withheld" (actuary selection and trust release), while the acceptability of investments and the withdrawal consent here carry no such qualifier. The differing treatment invites an argument about implied good faith.

The clause requires that Lincoln General "be a named party" to and "participate in the drafting and wording of" the reinsurance agreement without stating any standard or consequence if participation is refused. "Directly obligated" for amounts owed by the reinsurer to Santa Fe is a cut-through of uncertain scope.

"Default on its obligations" is not defined and "the amount of future losses forecast" gives no forecast period, so the collateral trigger and quantum are both left to argument. The $3 million cap is clear, but what sits beneath it is not.

"Those funds may be released" does not say whether the whole trust or only the excess over estimated remaining liability is released, nor who may compel a release. Read literally the entire $3 million could leave the trust the moment its value exceeds the actuarial estimate.

A release of the whole fund would defeat the Section II requirement that Santa Fe "provide security in the amount of $3 million" as security for the LPT, so the release mechanic and the security obligation pull against each other. Harmonising them requires reading in an excess-only limit.

"This release shall be performed annually" makes mandatory what the preceding sentence made permissive ("may be released"), and does not say from which date the year runs or who performs it. The mandatory/permissive mismatch is the point of contest.

The sentence cannot be squared with the immediately preceding release sentence of Section II, which says funds "may be released" only if the actuarial test is met, since an annual mandatory release would operate regardless. The two sentences of the same paragraph conflict.

"All activities in connection with the investigation, settlement, contesting, or handling of claims" is broad but the funding duty has no cap, term, or mechanism. The breadth is deliberate rather than ambiguous.

Santa Fe's open-ended funding duty here overlaps with its LPT liability under Section I and its ZBA reimbursement duty, raising a question whether the obligations are cumulative or the same money twice. Nothing expressly coordinates them.

The funding duty "shall include, but not be limited to, all claim payments, all attorney's fees, other legal expenses, and any other expenses related to claims investigation, settlement, contesting, and handling" sets a general catch-all against enumerated specifics. Whether "any other expenses" reaches items unlike the listed ones (e.g. defence of the Lawsuit itself, or administrative overhead) is a classic ejusdem generis question.

"Shall not affect any obligations of U.S. Auto, Gamma, or any other defendant" preserves obligations that are nowhere identified in this instrument, so the content of what is preserved is undeterminable from the MOU. The saving clause names no source agreement duty in particular.

Section X contemplates a settlement agreement providing "releases of all Defendants" upon Santa Fe's performance, which is difficult to square with this clause's preservation of every other defendant's obligations. A court could be asked which survives.

The instalment schedule is arithmetically consistent ($300,000 x 5 = $1.5 million) and dated, with no interest, acceleration or default term stated. The absence of a default remedy is a gap rather than an ambiguity.

Section IX makes refiling the lawsuit Lincoln General's remedy for non-completion, which raises the question whether missed instalments here are enforceable as a debt or only redressable by refiling. The two provisions must be read together.
The note must be "in a form substantially similar to Exhibit A," and "substantially similar" leaves the permissible deviation open. No Exhibit A appears with the executed instrument.

The referenced Exhibit A is not attached to or reproduced in the Memorandum of Understanding, so the incorporated form cannot be identified from the instrument itself. That makes the obligation's content depend on a document outside it.

The parties stipulate that the MOU "is sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement," a recital of legal effect that does not itself supply the missing terms of the LPT and settlement agreement it contemplates. Whether the stipulation makes an agreement to agree enforceable is squarely a question of construction.

The promise that the parties may "sue for its enforcement" cannot easily be reconciled with Section IX, which provides that on failure to complete the required actions "Lincoln's remedy shall be to refile the lawsuit." One clause grants an enforcement action on the MOU, the other appears to confine Lincoln to refiling.

"Tolling and other litigation resumption agreements" is a general catch-all after one specific, with no terms, deadline or form specified for the unnamed "other" agreements. Its reach cannot be determined from the words used.

Section VI already contains an operative tolling agreement of stated scope and duration, so whether the further "tolling agreements" promised here are a condition of the dismissal or mere confirmation of Section VI is unclear. The two provisions overlap without coordination.

The tolling runs "for five (5) years or until all claims ... have been paid and settled," and the disjunctive does not say whether the earlier or the later of the two periods governs. That single word decides whether the tolling ends in 2014 or continues indefinitely.

The clause tolls limitations on claims "otherwise related to" the reinsurance agreements and expressly extends to the "Other Causes of Action" in a separate April 28, 2008 letter agreement, whose terms are not in this instrument. Its scope therefore depends on a document the MOU does not reproduce.

"Subject to regulatory approval" does not identify the regulator, whose approval, of what, by when, or the consequence of refusal, and it is not said whether the approval is a condition precedent to formation or to performance. The phrase is capable of unmaking the whole bargain or none of it.

Making the MOU "and the matters to which it addresses" subject to regulatory approval sits awkwardly against Section V's stipulation that on execution the MOU is "sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement." Whether the instrument is presently binding depends on which prevails.

The heading covers failure to complete the required actions "or Later Breach," but the body addresses only inability to complete, so whether refiling is also the remedy for a later breach is unresolved; and "Lincoln's remedy shall be to refile the lawsuit" never says "sole" or "exclusive." Whether this is an exclusive remedy clause is the very thing to be construed.

The provision is very hard to reconcile with Section V, in which the parties agree the MOU "is sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement": if refiling is the exclusive remedy, the Section V enforcement right is largely nullified. Section IV's $1.5 million payment obligation is similarly left without a remedy.

The parties merely "agree to draft a settlement agreement" that will "among other things" provide releases, leaving the essential terms — scope of releases, timing, conditions — for later agreement. That is an agreement to agree on its face.

Releases of "all Defendants" based on Santa Fe's performance cannot be squared with Section III's statement that Santa Fe's funding "shall not affect any obligations of U.S. Auto, Gamma, or any other defendant." The two provisions point in opposite directions on the other defendants' exposure.

The particulars of the releases and "that agreement's other terms" are wholly deferred to a future document, so nothing in this sentence fixes what any party is released from. It defers rather than defines.

The deferral of all release particulars sits against Section V's stipulation that the MOU is already "sufficiently definite" to be sued on, since the central consideration for the defendants remains undetermined. The two must be read together.

"Such other and further documents and/or pleadings as may be reasonably necessary" sets no standard for what is reasonably necessary and could be read to compel execution of the LPT and settlement agreement themselves. Its outer edge is undefined.

If this further-assurances promise compels execution of the contemplated LPT and settlement agreement, it pulls against Section IX, which treats non-completion of those very documents as merely permitting Lincoln General to refile. The two allocate different consequences to the same failure.
